# Introduction

`ApproxOp` offers a unified computational interface for positive linear
approximation operators. This vignette demonstrates a reproducible workflow:
construct operators, approximate functions, compute and check moments,
quantify numerical errors, compare operator families, investigate parameters,
and register a custom operator.

The examples use version 0.1.0 of the package. The operator families shown
here use the `"discrete"` variant. Numerical results on finite grids are
diagnostics, not general approximation theorems.

```{r}
library(ApproxOp)
f <- function(x) x^2
grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 101)
```

# Constructing and evaluating Bernstein operators

For $x\in[0,1]$, the Bernstein operator is
$$
B_n(f;x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}{n\choose k}x^k(1-x)^{n-k}f(k/n).
$$

```{r}
B20 <- approx_operator(family = "bernstein", n = 20)
print(B20)
x <- c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75)
data.frame(x = x, exact = f(x),
           approximated = approximate(B20, f, x))
```

For the quadratic test function,
$$
B_n(t^2;x)=x^2+\frac{x(1-x)}{n}.
$$
This provides an independent analytic check.

```{r}
observed <- as.numeric(approximate(B20, f, x))
expected <- x^2 + x * (1-x)/20
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(observed, expected, tolerance = 1e-8)))
```

# Plotting approximation and error

```{r, fig.cap="Bernstein approximation of the quadratic function."}
plot(B20, f = f, grid = grid)
```

```{r, fig.cap="Pointwise Bernstein approximation error."}
plot(B20, f = f, grid = grid, type = "error")
```

# Moments and numerical verification

The first ordinary moments are $B_n(1;x)=1$, $B_n(t;x)=x$, and
$B_n(t^2;x)=x^2+x(1-x)/n$. In particular,
$\mu_{n,1}(x)=0$ and $\mu_{n,2}(x)=x(1-x)/n$.

```{r}
ordinary <- moments(B20, order = 2, x = x)
central <- moments(B20, order = 2, x = x, central = TRUE)
print(ordinary)
print(central)
```

```{r}
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(ordinary[, 3]),
                           x^2 + x*(1-x)/20, tolerance = 1e-8)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(central[, 3]),
                           x*(1-x)/20, tolerance = 1e-8)))
verify_moments(B20, order = 2, x = 0.5)
```

`verify_moments()` compares numerical calculation paths. Agreement alone is
not an independent mathematical proof; the explicit Bernstein formulas above
serve as separate benchmarks.

# Error analysis and convergence

The absolute error at a grid point is $|L_n(f;x)-f(x)|$.
`approx_error()` reports pointwise diagnostics.

```{r}
pointwise <- approx_error(B20, f, grid)
head(pointwise)
```

For $f(x)=x^2$, the exact uniform error of Bernstein approximation is
$1/(4n)$. Our grid includes $x=1/2$, where the maximum occurs.

```{r}
computed_max <- max(abs(as.numeric(approximate(B20, f, grid))-f(grid)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(computed_max, 1/(4*20), tolerance = 1e-8)))
data.frame(computed_max, analytic_max = 1/(4*20))
```

```{r}
degrees <- c(5, 10, 20, 40, 80)
conv <- convergence(B20, f = f, grid = grid, n = degrees)
print(conv)
data.frame(n = degrees, analytic_max_error = 1/(4*degrees))
```

```{r, fig.cap="Numerical convergence diagnostics for Bernstein operators."}
plot(conv)
```

# Comparing classical operator families

Bernstein operators are defined on $[0,1]$, whereas Szász--Mirakyan and
Baskakov operators act on $[0,\infty)$. Comparisons therefore use a common
grid inside $[0,1]$, without claiming uniform convergence on the entire
unbounded domain.

```{r}
S20 <- approx_operator(family = "szasz", n = 20)
K20 <- approx_operator(family = "baskakov", n = 20)
comparison <- compare_operators(
  operators = list(Bernstein = B20, Szasz = S20, Baskakov = K20),
  f = f, grid = grid, n = c(10, 20, 40)
)
print(comparison)
```

```{r, fig.cap="Comparison of approximation errors on the common grid."}
plot(comparison)
```

# Sheffer-based operators and parameter studies

The package also provides Sheffer-based subfamilies, including Appell,
Charlier, and Meixner. Each family has its own parameter restrictions;
consult the help pages before changing parameters.

The following Charlier example examines the effect of the parameter `a`
on the same finite evaluation grid.

```{r}
C20 <- approx_operator(
  family = "sheffer", subfamily = "charlier",
  n = 20, params = list(a = 2)
)
data.frame(x = x, Charlier = approximate(C20, f, x))
```

```{r}
scan <- parameter_scan(
  operator = C20, parameter = "a",
  values = c(1.5, 2, 3, 5),
  f = f, grid = grid
)
print(scan)
```

```{r, fig.cap="Charlier parameter scan."}
plot(scan)
```

For Meixner-based operators, admissible settings include
$0\leq\alpha\leq\beta$, $\theta>0$, and $1/2<c<1$.
These constraints are essential when designing parameter experiments.

# Registering a user-defined operator

To illustrate extensibility, consider
$$
Q_n(f;x)=\frac{n}{n+1}f(x)+\frac{1}{n+1}f(1/2),
\qquad x\in[0,1].
$$
This is a positive linear operator reproducing constants. Moreover,
$\|Q_nf-f\|_\infty\leq 2\|f\|_\infty/(n+1)$.

```{r}
register_operator(
  family = "example_average",
  domain = c(0, 1),
  evaluation_engine = function(f, x, operator) {
    n <- operator$n
    n/(n+1)*vapply(x, f, numeric(1)) +
      1/(n+1)*f(0.5)
  }
)
Q20 <- approx_operator(family = "example_average", n = 20)
data.frame(x = x, computed = approximate(Q20, f, x),
           exact_formula = 20/21*x^2 + 1/21*0.25)
```

```{r}
q_obs <- as.numeric(approximate(Q20, f, x))
q_exact <- 20/21*x^2 + 0.25/21
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(q_obs, q_exact, tolerance = 1e-8)))
```

The custom operator illustrates how the framework can be extended
without modifying its built-in operator families.

# Reproducibility and further reading

All examples above use deterministic functions and explicitly specified
evaluation grids. On machines with different numerical settings, minor
floating-point differences may occur. For more functions, consult
`help(package = "ApproxOp")` and the individual help pages.

```{r}
packageVersion("ApproxOp")
sessionInfo()
```
